description: Article-based learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway.

article.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
article.author: Ramit Sethi

cards.title: Spend Extravagantly on What You Love
cards.subtitle: Cut costs mercilessly on what you don't care about.
body: Figure out what you actually value and spend aggressively there. If you love coffee, don't cut the lattes.
Cut the things you buy out of habit that bring no joy. Money is a tool for living well.
cards.takeaway: Intentional spending on what matters beats universal frugality.

cards.title: Automate Everything
cards.subtitle: Willpower fails. Systems don't.
body: Manual money management requires constant decisions. Every paycheck becomes a negotiation with yourself.

• Automate savings and investments
• Money moves before you see it
• No decisions required
cards.takeaway: Automation removes the need for willpower in financial decisions.

cards.title: Big Wins Beat Small Cuts
cards.subtitle: Negotiating salary once adds thousands forever.
body: People obsess over $5 daily expenses while ignoring $5,000 annual decisions.
Negotiate salary once—it compounds your entire career. Focus on big wins; small stuff barely matters.
cards.takeaway: Major one-time decisions have more impact than daily micro-frugality.

cards.title: Credit Cards Are Tools, Not Traps
cards.subtitle: Used correctly, they offer free money. Used incorrectly, they're ruin.
body:
• Points and cash back
• Purchase protection
• Credit building
...but only if you pay in full monthly.
Carrying a balance negates all benefits. 20% interest erases any rewards instantly.
cards.takeaway: Credit cards reward discipline and punish its absence.

cards.title: Start Investing Now
cards.subtitle: Waiting until you understand everything costs more than learning by doing.
body: People delay investing because they want to learn first. Meanwhile, compound interest isn't waiting.
Start with index funds—simple, diversified, low-cost. A beginner's portfolio today beats an expert's in five years.
cards.takeaway: Imperfect action beats perfect paralysis in investing.

cards.title: Your 401(k) Match Is Free Money
cards.subtitle: Not getting the full match? You're declining a raise.
body: A 100% match means every dollar you contribute is immediately doubled. No investment can match that return.
Get the full match first. Everything else comes second.
cards.takeaway: Employer matching is the highest guaranteed return available.

cards.title: Spending Plans Beat Budgets
cards.subtitle: Budgets feel restrictive. A spending plan is permission.
body: Traditional budgets feel like punishment. A conscious spending plan starts with what you love.

• Fixed costs first
• Savings and investments
• Then guilt-free spending money
cards.takeaway: Frame your finances around permission, not restriction.

cards.title: Negotiate Everything
cards.subtitle: The sticker price is often just the opening offer.
body: Salary. Rent. Credit card rates. Bank fees. Medical bills. All negotiable.
A five-minute call can save hundreds. Worst case: they say no. Best case: changes your finances.
cards.takeaway: Asking for a better deal costs nothing and often works.

cards.title: Your Network Drives Your Net Worth
cards.subtitle: The people around you shape your financial expectations.
body: If your friends think investing is for rich people, you won't start.
Your reference group sets your financial normal. Upgrade your normal and the behaviors follow.
cards.takeaway: Financial habits are socially contagious—choose your influences.

cards.title: The $3 Question Doesn't Matter
cards.subtitle: Stop agonizing over small purchases.
body: Should you buy the coffee? The book? These decisions don't matter—it's not where money is won or lost.
The systems—automatic savings, investment allocations—these determine outcomes.
cards.takeaway: Small purchase decisions matter far less than automated systems.

cards.title: Rich Life Is Personal
cards.subtitle: Your version of rich isn't someone else's.
body: Rich might mean travel, early retirement, or freedom to quit a bad job. The definition is yours to choose.
Clarity on what rich means to you is prerequisite to getting there.
cards.takeaway: Define your own version of rich before optimizing for it.

cards.title: Financial Advice Is Often Wrong
cards.subtitle: Most advice is written for someone else's situation.
body: Generic advice assumes average circumstances. You have specific goals, constraints, and values.
Take principles, not prescriptions. The frameworks matter—the specific numbers are yours to set.
cards.takeaway: Adapt financial principles to your specific situation.
